title: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element, with every operation running in constant time.
keyPoints: Keep a parallel min stack whose top is always the current minimum, giving O(1) getMin.
On push, push the value to main and push min(value, currentMin) to the auxiliary stack.
On pop, pop both stacks in lockstep so the minimum stays correct as elements are removed.
For banking money, use BigDecimal and compareTo instead of primitive operators.
Space-optimized variant: push to min stack only when value <= current min; use <= not < for duplicates.
Delta-encoding variant uses a single stack but sacrifices readability for space.

s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a parallel min stack whose top is always the current minimum, so getMin is constant time.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Min Stack** – a stack augmented with an O(1) getMin operation that returns the current minimum element.
- **Two-stack design** – a main stack for values and an auxiliary stack where each entry is the minimum of all elements up to that level.
- **Push** – push the value onto main; push `min(value, currentMin)` onto the auxiliary stack.
- **Pop** – pop both stacks together to maintain alignment.
- **getMin** – peek the auxiliary stack in O(1).
- **Space** – O(n) extra for the auxiliary stack; optimized variant pushes only new minimums.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture a clerk at the National Bank of India stacking account balance slips. Next to the main spike she keeps a second spike of "smallest so far" slips. Every time she adds a balance, she also adds a slip showing the smallest balance seen up to that point. When she removes the top balance, she removes the matching smallest slip too. At any instant she can glance at the second spike and know the smallest balance on the stack.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Min Stack augments a normal stack with O(1) minimum retrieval by keeping a second auxiliary stack whose top always holds the current minimum. On push, I push the value onto the main stack and the smaller of the value and the current minimum onto the auxiliary. On pop, I pop both in lockstep. The getMin operation is a single peek.

The two-stack invariant is simple: at every level the auxiliary entry is the smallest value present from the bottom to that level. Popping in lockstep maintains this automatically. For banking money I use `BigDecimal` with `compareTo` rather than primitive operators to ensure correct scale and precision.

The space-optimized variant pushes to the min stack only on `<=` and pops only when the value matches the current minimum. The `<=` rather than `<` distinction is critical for handling duplicate minimums. A third approach encodes deltas in a single stack but sacrifices readability.

In my project at the National Bank of India, the risk dashboard tracks intraday balances as positions open and close, and the desk constantly needs the lowest balance for overdraft threshold checks. The min stack answers that in O(1) even as balances churn rapidly.

Remember one sentence: keep a parallel min stack in lockstep so the top is always the current minimum in O(1).
